summary: Sets out the IETF's policies on intellectual property rights such as patents in technologies it develops, and the goals of those policies. The aim is that participants know about IPR constraints early. It replaces RFC 3979 and RFC 4879 and updates RFC 2026.

plainLanguage.summary: When people work together on a standard, they share any patents or similar rights they own over the ideas they contribute. This document sets out when they must say so, where they file that, and what the working group does with the information once it arrives.

questions: do ietf participants have to disclose patents
subtitle: Who must tell the IETF about patents, when, and how, so working groups can choose technology with open eyes.

tldr.problem: A working group choosing between technical proposals needs to know early about any patent or similar claim that might cover them, but the IETF cannot judge whether such a claim is valid.
tldr.mechanism: Contributors and other participants must disclose IPR they reasonably and personally know covers a Contribution, as soon as reasonably possible, using the IETF's public disclosure process, with optional licensing terms that become irrevocable.
tldr.outcome: Working groups weigh disclosed IPR and licensing terms alongside technical merit, with no official preference among license types. The memo is BCP 79 and obsoletes RFC 3979 and RFC 4879.

facts.label: Update verification
facts.value: Three separate inquiries and at least 30 days

facts.label: Implementations needed to advance
facts.value: At least two independent, separate and successful uses of the licensing process

today: RFC 8179 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 79) published in May 2017, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It replaced RFC 3979 and RFC 4879; the companion policy on copyright and similar rights is RFC 5378.

sections.title: Goals and Three Basic Principles
sections.content:
The IETF policies on Intellectual Property Rights (IPR), such as patent rights, are designed so that working groups and participants have as much information as possible about any IPR constraints on a technical proposal as early as possible in the development process. The policies are meant to benefit the Internet community and the public at large while respecting the legitimate rights of IPR holders. This document updates RFC 2026 and, with RFC 5378, replaces Section 10 of it. It also obsoletes RFC 3979 and RFC 4879.

Three principles, originally outlined in Section 10 of RFC 2026, govern how the IETF deals with IPR claims. First, the IETF will make no determination about the validity of any particular IPR claim. Second, the IETF, following normal processes, can decide to use technology for which IPR disclosures have been made if it decides that such a use is warranted. Third, so that a working group can make an informed decision, all those contributing to its discussions must disclose the existence of any IPR the contributor or any other IETF participant believes covers or may ultimately cover the technology under discussion. This applies to contributors and to other participants, and applies whether they contribute in person, by email or by other means. It covers all IPR of the participant, the participant's employer, sponsor or others the participant represents that is reasonably and personally known to the participant. No patent search is required.

Copyright and trademark questions are handled separately in RFC 5378, and this document is not intended to address them. It is not intended as legal advice, and readers are advised to consult their own legal advisers for a legal interpretation of their rights.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF never rules on whether a patent claim is valid. What it asks for is that anyone who knows of a relevant claim says so early, so the working group can weigh the claim against the technical merits.

sections.title: Key Definitions
sections.content:
IPR means a patent, utility model or similar right that may cover an implementing technology, whether the right arises from a registration or renewal or from an application, in each case anywhere in the world. Covers means that a valid claim of a patent or patent application, including a provisional patent application, in any jurisdiction, or any other IPR, would necessarily be infringed by the exercise of a right such as making, using, selling, importing, distributing or copying with respect to an implementing technology. A valid claim is one of any unexpired patent or patent application that has not been withdrawn, cancelled or disclaimed, nor held invalid by a court of competent jurisdiction in an unappealed or unappealable decision. An Implementing Technology is a technology that implements an IETF specification or standard.

A Contribution is any submission to the IETF intended by the contributor for publication as all or part of an Internet-Draft or RFC, and any statement made within the context of an IETF activity, in each case intended to affect the IETF Standards Process or related to an Alternate Stream that has adopted the policy. Statements include oral statements and written and electronic communications addressed to any IETF plenary session, working group, birds of a feather session, WG design team, the IESG, the IAB, any IETF mailing list, web site, chat room or discussion board, or the RFC Editor. Statements made outside an IETF session, mailing list or other function, or clearly not intended as input to an IETF activity, are not Contributions. Invited plenary, area-meeting or research group presentations often cover background material and are not Contributions. The term written Contribution covers anything reduced to a written or visual form in any language and any media, permanent or temporary, including documents, email, discussion board postings, slides, text messages, instant messages and transcriptions of oral statements.

A Contributor is an individual submitting a Contribution. A Participant is any individual making a Contribution or otherwise acting to influence the outcome of a discussion relating to the IETF Standards Process. Acting as a Working Group Chair or Area Director counts as participating in all activities of the relevant working groups. Reasonably and personally known means something an individual knows personally or, because of the job the individual holds, would reasonably be expected to know. The wording is used to indicate that an organization cannot purposely keep an individual in the dark about patents or patent applications to avoid the disclosure requirement, but it does not require the contributor or participant, or the organization they represent, to perform a patent search.

An Alternate Stream is the IAB Document Stream, the IRTF Document Stream and the Independent Submission Stream, along with any future non-IETF streams. IETF Documents are RFCs and Internet-Drafts published as part of the IETF Standards Process.
sections.plainLanguage: A patent gives its owner the right to stop others building the thing it covers. The rule only asks what a person knows from their own job, so nobody has to go searching patent databases for what applies.

sections.title: Who Must Disclose and What Happens If They Do Not
sections.content:
Taking part in the IETF means being deemed to comply with this RFC. Three groups are involved. A Contributor who reasonably and personally knows of IPR meeting the conditions of Section 5.6 which the contributor believes covers or may ultimately cover a written Contribution intended as an input into the IETF Standards Process, or which the contributor reasonably and personally knows the employer or sponsor may assert against implementing technologies based on such a written Contribution, must disclose. An IETF Participant who knows of such IPR relating to someone else's written Contribution must also disclose. Anyone else is encouraged to make a voluntary disclosure, for example for third party IPR, or for IPR covering technology that does not yet meet the criteria for a Contribution such as something disclosed in an informal setting.

The duty applies to IPR that the person or their employer or sponsor owns directly or indirectly, can license or assert, derives a direct or indirect pecuniary benefit from, or on which the person is listed as an inventor. An obligation is also satisfied if the IPR owner, such as the employer, makes the disclosure instead.

There may be cases in which individuals are not permitted by their employers, or by other factors, to disclose the existence or substance of patent applications or other IPR. Since disclosure is required for anyone making a Contribution or participating in IETF activities, a person who is not willing or able to disclose IPR for this reason, or any other reason, must not contribute to or participate in IETF activities with respect to technologies that the person reasonably and personally knows may be covered by IPR which the person will not disclose, unless the person knows that the employer or sponsor will make the required disclosures on their behalf. Contributing or participating in IETF activities about a technology without making required IPR disclosures is a violation of IETF policy.

Besides any remedies or defences available to implementers and others under the law with respect to such a violation, sanctions are available through the normal IETF processes for handling disruptions to IETF work, as described in RFC 6701.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of person must file a disclosure: someone submitting their own text, and anyone else who knows of a claim over someone else’s text. Someone who cannot disclose should keep away from the technology in question.

sections.title: Making, Timing and Updating a Disclosure
sections.content:
Timely disclosure matters because working groups need as much information as they can while evaluating alternative solutions. A disclosure required under Section 5.1.1 must be made as soon as reasonably possible after the Contribution is submitted or made, unless the required disclosure is already on file. If the contributor first learns of IPR in the Contribution afterwards, for example a new patent application or the discovery of a relevant patent in a portfolio, a disclosure must be made as soon as reasonably possible after that IPR becomes reasonably and personally known. The Section 5.1.2 disclosure follows the same timing. Participants who realize that IPR may cover technology that will be or has been incorporated into a Contribution, or that is seriously being discussed in a working group, are strongly encouraged to make a preliminary disclosure as soon after coming to the realization as reasonably possible, rather than waiting until the Contribution is actually made.

Area Directors or persons assisting them may become aware of Contributions late in the process, for example at Last Call or during IESG review, and cannot reasonably be expected to disclose IPR covering those Contributions until they become aware of them.

Disclosures must follow the instructions at the IETF web site, and IPR disclosures and other IPR-related information, including licensing information, must not be included in RFCs or other Contributions. The RFC Editor removes any IPR-related information from Contributions before publication as an RFC.

A disclosure must include, to the extent reasonably available: the numbers of any issued patents or published patent applications, or an indication that it is based on unpublished applications; the names of the inventors; the specific IETF Documents or activity affected; and, if the document is an Internet-Draft, its specific version number. If it is not reasonably apparent which part of a document is allegedly covered, it is helpful to identify the sections said to be covered.

A disclosure must be updated promptly, or a new one made, after the publication of a previously unpublished patent application, the abandonment of an application, the issuance of a patent on a previously disclosed application, or a material change to the covered document that brings in additional IPR. If the application was abandoned, the new disclosure must explicitly withdraw the earlier ones based on it. Disclosures against a Contribution are assumed to be inherited by revisions of the Contribution and by any RFCs published from it, unless updated or withdrawn. If an IPR holder files patent applications in additional countries referring to substantially identical claims, no new or updated disclosure is required as a result of those filings or the patents issued on them. Any person may submit an update to an existing disclosure. If an update comes from someone other than the original submitter, the Secretariat tries to verify it with that submitter; if the submitter fails to respond after three separate inquiries and at least 30 days have passed since the initial inquiry, the Secretariat tells the updater that the update was not validated and requires legally sufficient evidence that the submitter, or their employer, owns or has the legal right to exercise control over the IPR.

A blanket statement that IPR may exist on every Contribution does not satisfy the requirement, nor does a blanket statement of willingness to license all such IPR under fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms. The requirement is satisfied by a blanket statement of the discloser's commitment to license all of its IPR meeting the requirements of Section 5.6 to implementers of an IETF specification on a royalty-free and otherwise reasonable and non-discriminatory basis, as long as any other terms and conditions are disclosed.
sections.plainLanguage: File the disclosure as soon as you know, using the IETF’s own process rather than a line inside the draft. Update it when a pending application is published, abandoned, or granted.

sections.title: Licensing Information and Its Binding Effect
sections.content:
A licensing declaration is not mandatory, but it is encouraged, because working groups use it when comparing one candidate technology against another. The useful thing to state is whether, once the IESG approves the specification for publication as an RFC, everyone will be able to implement it, use it, distribute it and exercise other rights over an implementing technology a) under a royalty-free and otherwise reasonable and non-discriminatory license, b) under a license with reasonable and non-discriminatory terms and conditions, which may carry a reasonable royalty or other payment, or c) with no need to obtain a license from the IPR holder at all, for example under a covenant not to sue, with or without defensive suspension. Where adding the declaration would hold the submission up significantly, the discloser may file without one and file a fresh disclosure once it is ready. A disclosure that volunteers text with licensing information, comments, notes or URLs may equally set out particular terms the holder intends to offer, maximum royalties included.

Because the IETF is likely to rely on licensing declarations, and implementers will make technical, legal and commercial decisions on the strength of such commitments, the people making the disclosure agree and acknowledge that the commitments and information it carries shall be irrevocable and will attach, to the extent permissible by law, to the associated IPR. Implementers are justified and entitled to rely on such materials in relation to that IPR, whether or not the IPR is later transferred to a third party by the person making the commitment. Holders making disclosures that contain licensing declarations or other such information must make sure the commitments bind any transferee of the relevant IPR, and that the transferee in turn uses reasonable efforts to bind a subsequent transferee, and so on. Licensing declarations must be made by people authorized to make them under Section 5.6.
sections.plainLanguage: A licensing promise made in a disclosure cannot be withdrawn later, and it survives the sale of the patent to somebody else. Implementers can rely on it.

sections.title: How Working Groups Weigh IPR
sections.content:
Working groups generally prefer technologies with no known IPR claims or, for technologies with claims against them, an offer of royalty-free licensing. To solve a given technical problem they have the discretion to adopt a technology against which IPR claims have been made if they feel it is superior enough to the alternatives to outweigh the potential cost of the licenses. Participants are expected to evaluate all the relevant tradeoffs from their perspective; most of the time these are based purely on technical excellence, but IPR considerations may also affect the evaluation and specific licensing terms may affect the participants' opinion of a technology's desirability.

The IETF has no official preference among different licensing terms beyond the preference stated at the beginning of the section. For information only, the document sets out some common conditions. When there is no commitment to license, that creates uncertainty. Where there is a commitment, the terms can still differ greatly, and the common conditions include terms that are fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory and may bear royalties or other financial obligations, known as FRAND or RAND; royalty-free terms that are otherwise fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory, known as RAND-z; and commitments not to assert declared IPR, possibly conditional on reciprocity. Open source projects often prefer the latter two. Licenses often come with complex terms that have to be evaluated in detail, so this crude classification may not be sufficient for a proper evaluation. For instance, licenses may also include reciprocity and defensive suspension requirements.

The level of use of a technology is also important. If technologies are being considered for a mandatory-to-implement change to a widely deployed protocol, the hurdle should be very high for encumbered technologies, whereas a similar hurdle for a new protocol could conceivably be lower. Working groups and areas may adopt stricter requirements in specific cases. The IETF Security Area has adopted stricter requirements for some security technologies, and it is common to have a mandatory-to-implement security technology in IETF specifications so that at least one common security technology is present in all implementations. An IETF consensus has developed that no mandatory-to-implement security technology can be specified unless it has no known IPR claims against it or a royalty-free license is available to implementers of the specification. It is possible to specify such a technology in violation of this principle if there is a very good reason to do so and that reason is documented and agreed to through IETF consensus. The limitation does not extend to other security technologies in the same specification if they are not listed as mandatory to implement.

Two cautions close the section. The absence of IPR disclosures at any given time is not the same as knowing there will be no IPR disclosure in the future, or that no IPR covers the relevant technology; people or organizations not currently involved in the IETF can file disclosures at any time. And the existence of a disclosure should not be taken to mean the disclosed IPR is valid or enforceable or actually covers a particular Contribution. Although the IETF can make no determination of validity, enforceability or applicability, it is reasonable for individuals in a working group or the IESG to take their own views into account when evaluating alternatives.
sections.plainLanguage: Working groups prefer designs nobody has claimed, or ones offered for free. They can still pick a claimed design if it is clearly better. Security features that every device must support face a much higher bar.

sections.title: Change Control, Advancement and Other Streams
sections.content:
The IETF must have change control over the technology described in any Standards Track IETF Document, so that it can fix problems that may be discovered or produce other derivative works. In some cases the developer of patented or otherwise controlled technology may decide to hand over to the IETF the right to evolve the technology. Implementing an agreement between the IETF and that developer can be complex; RFC 1790 and RFC 2339 are examples. There is no inherent prohibition against a Standards Track IETF Document making a normative reference to proprietary technology; a number of IETF standards support proprietary cryptographic transforms.

To advance a standard, RFC 6410 states that if the technology required to implement the specification requires patented or otherwise controlled technology, then the set of implementations must demonstrate at least two independent, separate and successful uses of the licensing process. The key word is requires: the mere existence of disclosed IPR does not necessarily mean that licenses are actually required in order to implement the technology.

The IESG will not make any determination that any terms for the use of an implementing technology, such as an assurance of reasonable and non-discriminatory terms, have been fulfilled in practice. It applies the normal requirements for the advancement of Internet Standards. If the two unrelated implementations required to advance from Proposed Standard to Internet Standard were produced by different organizations or individuals, or if the significant implementation and successful operational experience required for that advance has been achieved, the IESG will presume the terms are reasonable and to some degree non-discriminatory. This also applies where multiple implementers have concluded that no licensing is required. The presumption may be challenged at any time, including during the Last Call period.

IETF Documents must not contain any mention of specific IPR; all specific disclosures are filed as described in Section 5, and readers are pointed to the IETF's online IPR list. The rules apply to documents in the IETF Document Stream. The rules for Alternate Streams are set by the managers of those streams, currently the IAB, the Internet Research Steering Group and the Independent Submission Editor, who may elect through their own internal processes to apply this document. If a manager adopts it, they must do so publicly and notify their contributors. The Security Considerations section notes that there are no known issues of security with IPR procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The team must be able to fix and evolve the finished specification, even where a patent is involved. These rules cover the IETF’s own work, and other groups may adopt them.

sections.title: What Changed Since RFC 3979 and RFC 4879
sections.content:
Section 13 reviews what changed since RFC 3979 and is informational only; the text of Sections 1 to 12 prevails, and any discrepancy is resolved in favour of it. The material in RFC 3979 was reorganised substantially to produce this document, and this section does not describe that reorganisation. Boilerplate was deleted because it had moved to the Trust Legal Provisions.

New definitions include Alternate Stream and Participating in an IETF discussion or activity. Contribution now requires that a statement be intended to affect the IETF Standards Process, so that informational presentations such as guest speakers are not Contributions, and it now lists birds of a feather sessions, design teams, web sites and chat rooms. Covers now includes provisional patent applications. The IPR definition no longer refers to copyrights, database rights and data rights, since copyright is handled in RFC 5378 and is treated very differently from patents.

The trigger for a Section 5.1.1 disclosure changed from publication of a Contribution in an Internet-Draft to the Contribution being submitted or made, and the disclosure obligation was limited to written Contributions intended as inputs to the Standards Process, with oral contributions handled separately in the new Section 5.7. The wording of blanket IPR statements changed from willingness to commitment, so a blanket disclosure without specific patent numbers is not compliant unless the discloser commits to license such patents royalty-free and otherwise reasonably. Section 5.4.2 gained significant detail about updating disclosures, including on issuance of patents, amendment of claims, an employee changing jobs, and an employer acquiring another company, while clarifying that no new disclosure is needed for foreign counterparts. A new paragraph in Section 5.5 makes licensing declarations irrevocable, and another requires them to be made by authorized people. Section 5.6 was extended to cover a participant who derives a pecuniary benefit from the IPR or is a listed inventor. Section 6 gained language about potential remedies for failures to disclose. Section 7 gained paragraphs on how working groups evaluate disclosures, including the stricter rule for mandatory-to-implement security technology, which can only be violated with IETF consensus. A new Section 11 gives Alternate Stream managers a procedure for adopting these rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The wording was tightened. The new text says more clearly who counts as taking part, which kinds of ideas the policy covers, and how a disclosure gets updated.

items.title: No validity ruling
items.text: The IETF will make no determination about the validity of any particular IPR claim.

items.title: Use is allowed
items.text: The IETF can decide to use technology for which IPR disclosures have been made if it decides that such a use is warranted.

items.title: Disclose what you know
items.text: Contributors and other participants disclose IPR they believe covers the technology. No patent search is required.

viz.caption: THE LICENSING OPTIONS A DISCLOSURE MAY STATE (SECTION 5.5.A)

items.label: Royalty-free
items.desc: A royalty-free and otherwise reasonable and non-discriminatory license.

items.label: Reasonable terms
items.desc: Reasonable and non-discriminatory terms and conditions, including a reasonable royalty or other payment.

items.label: No license needed
items.desc: No license is needed from the IPR holder, for example a covenant not to sue with or without defensive suspension.

cells: Terms that are fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory and may bear royalties or other financial obligations.
Royalty-free terms that are otherwise fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory.
A commitment not to assert declared IPR, possibly conditional on reciprocity.

items.title: Patent numbers
items.text: The numbers of any issued patents or published patent applications, or an indication that the disclosure rests on unpublished applications.

items.title: Inventor names
items.text: The names of the inventors, for issued patents and published patent applications.

items.title: Affected document
items.text: The specific IETF Document or activity affected.

items.title: Draft version
items.text: The specific version number, if the IETF Document is an Internet-Draft.
